The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$, curvature tensors
$R^{a}{}_{bcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, scalar curvature $S$ and Einstein
tensor $G_{ab}$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). Let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, let $K\subseteq U$ be compact, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
open interval with $0\in I$, and let $s\mapsto g(s)$, $s\in I$, be a family of
smooth Lorentzian metrics of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $M$ such that

- $g(0)=g$ and $g(s)=g$ on $M\setminus K$ for every $s\in I$; and
- the components $g(s)_{ab}$ in the chart are smooth functions of $(s,x)$ on
  $I\times x(U)$ ([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]).

Write $h_{ab}:=\partial_sg(s)_{ab}|_{s=0}$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field with support in $K$, and
$q^{ab}:=\partial_sg(s)^{ab}|_{s=0}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]).

**(a) Variation of the inverse metric; realizability.** $q^{ab}
=-g^{ac}g^{bd}h_{cd}$; conversely, for every smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h_0$ with compact support in $U$ there is $\lambda_0>0$ such
that for every $|\lambda|<\lambda_0$ the family $s\mapsto g+s\lambda h_0$
satisfies the hypotheses above on the parameter interval $(-1,1)$ (with
$K=\operatorname{supp}h_0$). In particular any prescribed smooth compactly
supported inverse-metric direction $q$ is realized by $g+s h$ on a
sufficiently small interval, with $h_{ab}=-g_{ac}g_{bd}q^{cd}$.

**(b) Variation of the Christoffel symbols.** The field
$\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_s\Gamma(s)^{a}{}_{bc}|_{s=0}$ is a smooth
tensor field on $U$ and

$$\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{ad}\bigl(\nabla_bh_{cd}+\nabla_ch_{bd}-\nabla_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(c) Variation of the Ricci tensor (Palatini identity).**
$\delta\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\partial_s\operatorname{Ric}(s)_{bd}|_{s=0}$
satisfies

$$\delta\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\nabla_a\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{db}-\nabla_d\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{ab}.$$

**(d) Variation of the curvature density.** With
$V^{a}:=g^{bd}\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{db}-g^{ab}\delta\Gamma^{d}{}_{db}$ and
$w(s):=\sqrt{|\det(g(s)_{ab})|}$ the metric density of
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]],

$$\partial_s\bigl(w(s)S(s)\bigr)\big|_{s=0}=w\,G_{ab}q^{ab}+\partial_a\bigl(wV^{a}\bigr).$$

**(e) Variation of the chart action integral.** For every constant
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, the function
$F(s):=\int_U\bigl[(S(s)-2\Lambda)w(s)-(S(0)-2\Lambda)w(0)\bigr]\,d^4x$ is the compactly supported chart action difference, differentiable at $0$, and

$$F'(0)=\int_U\bigl(G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}\bigr)q^{ab}\,w\,d^4x,$$

where the integrand is compactly supported in $K$ and the integral is an
ordinary Riemann integral in the chart coordinates
([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]).

**(f) Variation of the timelike length and particle action.** Let
$\gamma:[a,b]\to U$ and $H$ be as in
[[lem-gr-first-variation-of-proper-time]], so that $\gamma$ is $C^2$, future
timelike, parametrized with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-c^2$, the variation is $C^2$
with fixed endpoints and future timelike fibres, and $L(s)$ is the length
functional of that lemma. Then the first-variation formulas (1)-(3) of that
lemma hold verbatim. Consequently for every $m>0$ the particle action
$S_p(\gamma):=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))}\,dt$ satisfies
$\partial_sS_p(H(s,\cdot))|_{s=0}=-mc\,L'(0)$, so within this class of curves
and variations $\gamma$ is stationary for $S_p$ if and only if
$D_t\gamma'=0$, i.e. if and only if $\gamma$ is a geodesic in its proper-time
parameter ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and fix a conversion constant $c>0$, let $[a,b]$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, let $X:[a,b]	o A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), and let $\mathcal A$ be a $C^2$ covector field on a neighbourhood of the image of $X$. An inertial frame is $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with future positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal basis, and its chart sends $p$ to the unique coordinates of $p-o$ in that basis; in these coordinates $\eta_{\mu
u}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{\mu
u}$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). In any such chart write the covector components as $A_\mu$ and define the antisymmetric covariant field $F$ by $F_{
u\mu}=\partial_
u A_\mu-\partial_\mu A_
u$; this coordinate formula defines the notation $F=d\mathcal A$ used below. Indices run from $0$ to $3$, repeated indices are summed, and $U_
u=\eta_{
u\mu}U^\mu$. All integrals in this particle lemma are finite-interval Riemann integrals. On $[a,b]$, $C^2$ means continuous components and continuous first and second derivatives with their one-sided endpoint values; equations at endpoints use those same one-sided derivatives. For fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations $h:[a,b]	o V$ with $h(a)=h(b)=0$ and for $m,c>0$ and real $q$ consider

$$S[X]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,ds+q\int_a^bA_\mu(X)\dot X^\mu\,ds .$$

Then for each such $h$ the curve $X+\varepsilon h$ remains future timelike for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$, and stationarity of $S$ under all such variations is equivalent to

$$m rac{dU_
u}{d	au}=qF_{
u\mu}U^\mu,\qquad rac{d	au}{ds}= rac{\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}}c,\qquad F=d\mathcal A,$$

where $	au(s)=	au_0+c^{-1}\int_a^s\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,dr$ with arbitrary $	au_0\in\mathbb R$, and $U(s)=\dot X(s)/	au\prime(s)$ are the proper-time function and four-velocity ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]); $dU/d	au=U\prime/	au\prime$ and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). This is a calculation about the chosen functional; adopting it as a physical particle action is an additional model assumption, and it makes no existence claim for coupled singular particles and fields. The coefficient-localization proof below is one-dimensional and choice-free; it does not invoke an AC-qualified Lebesgue fundamental lemma.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

The **real numbers** are the quotient ring

$$\mathbb{R} := \mathcal{C} / \mathcal{N}$$

of the ring of Cauchy sequences ([[thm-cauchy-ring]]) by the ideal of null
sequences ([[lem-null-ideal]]). The class of $(a_n)$ is written
$[(a_n)]$. Each rational $q$ maps to the class $\hat q$ of the constant
sequence $(q, q, q, \dots)$.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$

   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in

The components in an orthonormal tetrad have tesla units. This is an explicit curved-background model input. The cited EM supplier is a flat Minkowski definition and does not derive a curved field or curved Maxwell system.
- On any open potential domain where a $C^2$ covector field $A$ exists, $F=dA$ with components $F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ and $A$ has tesla metre components in the stated coordinates. No global potential is assumed, and no Maxwell equation or constitutive law is imposed here.

This is a test-body model on a fixed background: self-gravity, gravitational backreaction, self-field evaluation, radiation reaction, collisions, electric dipole moments, field-gradient translational forces and higher multipoles are outside this definition. Units follow the framework-local SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and do not identify quantities across frameworks.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure, as required for the metric-selected Levi–Civita connection $\nabla$ of [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Let $O\subseteq M$ be open and let $A$ be a $C^2$ covector field on $O$; define the $C^1$ two-form $F=dA$ by $F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ in each chart. Fix constants $c>0$, $m>0$ and $q\in\mathbb R$. Let $z:[a,b]\to O$ be a $C^2$ future-directed timelike curve, where $a<b$ are proper-time values in seconds and $U=dz/d\tau$ satisfies $g(U,U)=-c^2$. For every $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variation $z_\epsilon$ through timelike curves in $O$, with variation field $J=\partial_\epsilon z_\epsilon|_{\epsilon=0}$ and $J(a)=J(b)=0$, define

$$S[z_\epsilon]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(\partial_\tau z_\epsilon,\partial_\tau z_\epsilon)}\,d\tau+q\int_a^b A(\partial_\tau z_\epsilon)\,d\tau.$$

Then the first variation is

$$\delta S=\int_a^b\left[-m\,g(J,\nabla_UU)+qF(J,U)\right]d\tau.$$

Consequently, $z$ is stationary under all local chart-supported fixed-endpoint variations if and only if

$$m(\nabla_UU)_a=qF_{ab}U^b,$$

equivalently $m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U)$, where $F^\sharp(v)$ is defined by $g(F^\sharp(v),w)=F(w,v)$. The statement is local to a potential domain; no global potential is assumed.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Let $I=[a,b]$ and $J=[\tilde a,\tilde b]$ be compact nondegenerate real intervals, let $\phi:J\to I$ be an admissible parameter change from [A1], and let $h:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. By [F5], $h$ is integrable. Define $H(x):=\int_a^x h(s)\,ds$; [F6] gives $H'=h$ on $I$, with one-sided derivatives at its endpoints. The chain rule [F3] applied to $G:=H\circ\phi$ gives $G'(\lambda)=h(\phi(\lambda))\phi'(\lambda)$ on $J$. This derivative is continuous by [F4] and therefore integrable by [F5]. Since $\phi(\tilde a)=a$ and $\phi(\tilde b)=b$, [F7] yields $\int_{\tilde a}^{\tilde b}h(\phi(\lambda))\phi'(\lambda)\,d\lambda=G(\tilde b)-G(\tilde a)=H(b)-H(a)=\int_a^b h(s)\,ds$. Thus the one-dimensional integral substitution used below holds for each continuous action integrand.

The segment in the statement is parameterized by proper time, and [A1] admits $\lambda=\tau$. If the same segment and variations are expressed in any other admissible parameter, step 2.1 proves that both the action and fixed-endpoint stationarity are unchanged. Therefore it suffices to test stationarity with $\lambda=\tau$. Under [A2], the curve, potential, regularity and endpoint hypotheses now match the local first-variation result [F2].

For any local fixed-endpoint variation $\gamma_\epsilon:[a,b]\to O$ from [A1], composition with $\phi$ gives a $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variation $\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi$ on $J$. In chart components, for $\widetilde\gamma^i(\epsilon,\lambda):=\gamma^i(\epsilon,\phi(\lambda))$, the first and second derivatives in $\lambda$ are $(\partial_s\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,\phi'$ and $(\partial_{ss}\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,(\phi')^2+(\partial_s\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,\phi''$; the derivatives in $\epsilon$ and the mixed derivative are $(\partial_\epsilon\gamma^i)\circ\phi$, $(\partial_{\epsilon\epsilon}\gamma^i)\circ\phi$ and $(\partial_{\epsilon s}\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,\phi'$. The chain and product rules [F3], together with continuity under composition and products [F4], show these derivatives are continuous, so the family remains $C^2$. Since $\phi'>0$, the composed curves remain future timelike and have the same endpoint events, and the chart-supported variation field remains supported in that chart. Bilinearity of $g$ gives $\sqrt{-g((\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi)',(\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi)')}=(\sqrt{-g(\gamma_\epsilon',\gamma_\epsilon')})\circ\phi\,\phi'$, and linearity of the covector $A$ gives $A((\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi)')=(A(\gamma_\epsilon'))\circ\phi\,\phi'$. Both scalar integrands are continuous by [F4]; applying step 1.1 to each proves $S[\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi]=S[\gamma_\epsilon]$ for every $\epsilon$. Composition with $\phi^{-1}$ is the inverse map on variation families. Thus the action functions and their first variations agree, so stationarity is invariant under every admissible reparameterization.
